title: Mooers v. Middlebury College
lead: A student seeking a pandemic tuition refund failed to plead a specific promise of continued campus instruction, but his alternative unjust-enrichment claim survived because no contract term yet governed retention of the disputed payments.

actors.name: Henry Mooers
actors.role: Middlebury undergraduate and proposed class representative

actors.name: Judge Christina Reiss
actors.role: District judge deciding the amended complaint’s sufficiency

proceedings: Original dismissal motion superseded by amendment and denied as moot; court dismissed contract, conversion, and consumer-protection counts, allowed unjust enrichment to proceed, and gave twenty days for another amendment.
limits: This is the September 2021 pleading decision. No refund, damages, restitution, or class certification was ordered. The casebook’s 2022 description is separate later history, not part of this ruling or a complete subsequent-history review.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The spring semester began on campus and moved online
sections.cue: Introduce the payments and alleged promises before the closure.
paragraphs: Henry Mooers was a Middlebury College undergraduate. He and the proposed class paid approximately $28,940 in tuition and $218 in student-activity fees for the spring 2020 semester, scheduled from February 10 through May 19. Mooers alleged that publications and statements during application, enrollment, registration, and payment promised an on-campus educational experience. He said he chose Middlebury over another institution or an online-only university in reliance on them.

The cited materials described immersive learning, an inclusive campus, residential community, shared facilities, and education inside and outside classrooms. His complaint included Instagram images of students with professors, in dormitories, and studying on campus; descriptions of the arts center, library, and academic facilities; and presidential statements about the campus experience.

Middlebury held no in-person undergraduate classes after March 13, 2020, and instruction continued remotely. Mooers alleged loss of libraries, laboratories, study rooms, face-to-face interaction, extracurricular activities, health and fitness facilities, sporting events, and commencement. Students requested refunds, but tuition was not refunded. He characterized the remote service as materially different from what students bought. Those assertions were allegations assessed at pleading, not trial findings.

sections.title: Mooers pursued four theories, and the college moved to dismiss
sections.cue: Establish the amended pleading and the limits of the decision.
paragraphs: Mooers sued for himself and a proposed class, seeking disgorgement and prorated tuition and mandatory-fee refunds for the period without in-person services. He asserted breach of contract, unjust enrichment, conversion, and violation of the Vermont Consumer Protection Act.

Middlebury moved to dismiss the original complaint on January 22, 2021. After a stipulation permitting amendment, Mooers amended on March 12, and the college filed a new Rule 12(b)(6) motion on April 12. Judge Christina Reiss heard argument July 20 and ruled September 16. The new pleading and motion made the first motion moot.

The court accepted well-pleaded facts and favorable reasonable inferences, not conclusory recitations of elements, and did not weigh evidence or predict ultimate success. At argument, Mooers asked for separate treatment of activity fees, but the amended complaint had not yet identified those fees as a distinct contractual obligation.

sections.title: The alleged wrong could be examined without grading educational quality
sections.cue: Resolve the threshold defense before testing the promise itself.
paragraphs: Middlebury argued that comparing online and in-person education would require judicial evaluation of academic quality. The court distinguished enforcement of an alleged undertaking from educational malpractice. A court could ask what services were promised and delivered without judging curricula, teaching methods, materials, or individual achievement. References to value and possible damages comparisons did not necessarily transform the claimed failure to deliver a service into negligent education.

That threshold conclusion did not establish a contract breach. Both parties accepted a contractual relationship, but Mooers still needed to identify the particular undertaking. Vermont law allowed brochures, catalogs, and official statements to supply terms. General aspirations and descriptions of ordinary campus life, however, did not necessarily promise particular services through extraordinary circumstances.

The court compared Patel, another university-refund case in which different prices for online and campus courses and concrete catalog and contractual language supported an in-person commitment. Mooers’s descriptions and images lacked that specificity. They did not plausibly promise the asserted campus services even during a pandemic. The court therefore dismissed the contract count. It did not first find an unambiguous promise and then excuse performance through impossibility or force majeure; it found the pleaded duty insufficiently identified.

sections.title: Unjust enrichment asked a different question about keeping the payments
sections.cue: Explain why an admitted relationship did not yet foreclose the alternative.
paragraphs: Vermont unjust enrichment required a conferred benefit, acceptance, and circumstances making retention inequitable. Mooers alleged payment for services and activities not received. That stated a plausible alternative without requiring the specific promise missing from his contract claim.

A valid, enforceable contract governing the subject ordinarily displaces quasi-contract recovery. But Middlebury identified no term allocating payments when the college closed or moved exclusively online. Rule 8(d)(3) and Vermont law allowed inconsistent alternatives while the agreement’s scope remained unresolved. A later factual record could establish a governing term that defeated restitution; the decision did not authorize overriding an unfavorable bargain.

Nor did survival of this count establish the amount or existence of unjust enrichment. Whether remote instruction offset the claimed loss, how to value any retained benefit, and whether keeping the payments was ultimately unjust remained undecided.

sections.title: The refund policy and affirmative defenses did not resolve that uncertainty
sections.cue: Keep the record rule separate from the policy’s substantive scope.
paragraphs: Middlebury relied on a refund policy, but it was not incorporated into, referenced by, or integral to the amended complaint, and the college had not requested judicial notice. It was therefore outside the materials properly considered on this dismissal motion. Even if considered, it addressed voluntary withdrawal or dropping below a full course load, not a college closure or exclusive online instruction during a pandemic. Neither reason established that all institutional refund policies were unenforceable.

The college also argued that payment and continued participation ratified its performance and waived objections. Waiver and ratification were affirmative defenses; a plaintiff ordinarily did not have to anticipate and plead around them. Their possible existence did not defeat the unjust-enrichment pleading.

sections.title: The remaining counts lacked their own required allegations
sections.cue: Explain the conversion and deception rulings separately.
paragraphs: Conversion required specific property over which Mooers retained a superior possessory right. His demand identified an obligation to repay part of an amount spent, not segregated money or a documentary intangible. Tuition and fees were presumably commingled. That deficiency defeated conversion. The court expressly declined to decide Middlebury’s additional economic-loss defense.

The Vermont Consumer Protection Act required a material representation, omission, or practice likely to mislead a reasonable consumer. The court accepted that Middlebury arguably acted in commerce rather than declaring colleges categorically exempt. But its statements did not plausibly promise unchanged on-campus services during a pandemic, so disappointed expectations did not establish consumer deception. A mere breach also did not establish consumer fraud, although contractual dealings could involve separately deceptive conduct; the remedies were not invariably mutually exclusive.

sections.title: The order left one claim pending and allowed another attempt to plead
sections.cue: End with each count’s disposition and the absence of a refund award.
paragraphs: On September 16, 2021, Reiss granted dismissal of contract, conversion, and consumer protection—Counts 1, 3, and 4—and denied dismissal of unjust enrichment, Count 2. The earlier motion was denied as moot. Because amendment was not yet shown futile and no other reason justified denial, Mooers received twenty days to file a second amended complaint.

The court ordered no refund, restitution, damages, or class certification. It allowed an alternative theory to proceed and another pleading to be filed. The casebook separately describes a 2022 ruling in which new tuition allegations remained inadequate while a more distinct activity-fee contract claim survived; that was later procedural history, not this September 2021 judgment.
